input:
Scope
This review takes an in-depth look at membrane separations for solvent recovery, drawing on a body of some 135 papers published over the last 13 years. Solvent recovery by means of membrane separation is an approach that returns a process solvent back to the process, either in place of a conventional distillation step or positioned just ahead of one, and the papers that are covered here report on this particular duty across a wide and varied range of different solvents and membrane materials. Two classes of membrane dominate the record. Polymeric membranes, which are cast as flat sheets or spun as hollow fibres, account for the bulk of the reported work, while ceramic membranes account for a smaller share, at a higher purchase price, in return for a wider tolerance of aggressive solvents and of cleaning at temperature. The separations themselves broadly fall into two groups according to the species that is being retained: separations that retain a dissolved product, a catalyst or a dissolved impurity while the solvent itself passes through, and separations that retain larger species such as polymers, oils and suspended matter from within a solvent stream. The reports in the literature come from laboratory cells, from pilot installations and from a smaller number of fully operating plant installations, and these three settings do not report performance in the same terms. The review is confined to separations in which the membrane itself does the separation work, and hybrid arrangements, in which a membrane unit treats the product of a distillation or feeds into one, are only really covered where the membrane duty happens to be reported on its own terms.

Established results
A number of findings are well established across the record. Chief among them is the trade-off between permeance and rejection. A membrane that allows solvent to pass through it more quickly will almost invariably retain less of the dissolved species, and no reported membrane manages to escape this trade-off; reported development work tends to move along the trade-off rather than removing it. Retention increases with the size of the dissolved species relative to the pores of the membrane, and the retention of a species well below the pore size is weak in every solvent reported. Swelling of a polymeric membrane in a solvent changes both quantities at the same time: a swollen membrane will pass solvent more quickly while retaining less, and the change is determined by the particular pairing of membrane polymer and solvent rather than by either of them on its own. Concentration polarisation at the surface of the membrane is also well established as a standing limitation on measured performance, since the layer of retained species that builds at the surface reduces the solvent flux and changes the composition the membrane itself sees, and reported comparisons that stir or flow the feed more quickly demonstrate this effect directly. Ceramic membranes hold their performance in solvents that would swell or dissolve polymeric membranes, and the record on that point is consistent. Finally, fouling of the membrane by material present in the feed is established as the normal limiting factor on run length between cleanings, in plant reports and laboratory reports alike.

Disagreements
One of the most significant areas of disagreement in the record concerns the decline in permeance that takes place during extended operation, and this is the largest conflict in the literature. One set of reports finds that permeance falls early in a run and then settles, holding a steady value for the remainder of the run. A second set of reports, by contrast, finds that the permeance goes on falling for just as long as the run is followed, with no settled value ever being reached. The two sets are in agreement about the early fall but disagree about what actually follows it. The cause assigned to the decline also differs between the sets. Reports in the first set tend to assign the early fall to compaction of the membrane under pressure, and treat the settled value as being the working permeance. Reports in the second set tend to assign the continuing fall either to fouling that the cleaning process does not fully reverse, or to a slow change taking place in the membrane material while it is in contact with the solvent. This disagreement cannot be settled from the published record, largely because the two sets describe different run lengths, different cleaning histories and different feed compositions, and a report that follows one membrane through repeated cycles of operation and cleaning, in one solvent at one duty, is rare. Until such time as reports routinely state run length and cleaning history alongside permeance, the conflict will remain as much a conflict of reporting practice as a conflict about actual behaviour.

Gaps
The most striking gap is the measurement nobody reports: the permeance of the membrane after cleaning, tracked over repeated cycles of operation and cleaning. Cleaning is reported simply as an event: a membrane is cleaned and returned to service, and the run that follows is described. What is not given is the permeance the cleaning recovers, stated against the permeance of the new membrane and against the permeance at the end of the preceding run. Without that particular measurement, the published record simply cannot distinguish between a membrane that is slowly being fouled beyond the point of recovery and a membrane that is being cleaned back to its normal working state on each and every occasion, and the disagreement about permeance decline cannot properly be resolved. A second gap follows from the first. Plant reports tend to state production outcomes for a recovery unit as a whole and seldom separate the membrane duty from the duties around it, so the operating record that would test the laboratory findings at scale is not in the published literature. The review therefore closes on the position that the record as a whole supports: membrane separation does recover solvents at the duties that have been reported, within a permeance and rejection trade-off that development work has not removed, with the long-run behaviour of the membrane still unresolved for want of that one missing measurement.
